Modified assessment: The statement is hawkish overall. While it notes robust job gains and low unemployment, it emphasizes “elevated” inflation, cites war- and pandemic-related supply shocks, raises the target range to 4.25–4.50%, and signals “ongoing increases” plus continued balance-sheet runoff. In the Taylor-rule framework, inflation above target warrants a more restrictive stance, and explicit forward guidance about further hikes tightens conditions beyond the contemporaneous move (Federal Reserve utilizes Forward Guidance; implements Taylor Rule). Literature identifying monetary policy shocks (Romer and Romer; Bernanke and Mihov) associates such tightening with near-term output headwinds, consistent with the text’s focus on inflation risks. The operational details—higher interest on reserve balances and ON RRP, and QT caps—reinforce contractionary pressure via the reserves and term-structure channels (Federal Reserve introduced Interest on Reserves in 2008; utilizes Quantitative Easing/Balance Sheet tools; Cochrane and Piazzesi on yield-curve sensitivity). Given supply-side drivers (pandemic and the Ukraine war) that worsen the inflation-output trade-off, the Committee’s strong commitment to 2% (inflation targeting) underscores resolve but adds to near-term restrictive tone. Netting modest growth language against the dominant anti-inflation stance, the sentiment tilts moderately negative.
